title: Damping, forced oscillations and resonance; Temperature, internal energy, thermal equilibrium; Specific heat capacity and latent heat; Gas laws and ideal gas equation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: T01-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; T01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; O04-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game; T01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: O04-uk1#N.3, T01-1#N.2, T01-uk1#N.2, T02-1#N.3a, T02-uk1#N.9, T05-1#N.2a, O04-uk1#N.5, T01-1#N.5, T01-uk1#N.5, T02-1#N.6, T02-uk1#N.10b, T05-1#N.6.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Thermal equilibrium
items.clue: Condition of bodies in contact with no net energy transfer between them.

items.label: Temperature
items.clue: Property that decides which way net energy flows between two bodies in contact.

items.label: Light damping
items.clue: Condition in which the amplitude falls by roughly the same fraction on every cycle.

items.label: Internal energy
items.clue: Total of the random kinetic and potential contributions of all the particles in a body.

questions.stem: A lightly damped mass–spring system is released with an amplitude of 60 mm. After one complete oscillation its amplitude is 45 mm. The amplitude falls by the same fraction in each oscillation. What is the amplitude after three complete oscillations?

options.text: 15 mm
25 mm
34 mm
30 mm

questions.explanation: Each amplitude is 0.75 × the previous one: 60 × 0.75³ = 25 mm.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?

options.text: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.
From the block to the water, until they have equal internal energies.

questions.stem: Gas is sealed in a cylinder whose walls and piston are insulated. The gas pushes the piston outward quickly, and the temperature of the gas falls. Which statement explains the fall?

options.text: The gas was cooled: energy left it because of a temperature difference with the piston.
The gas did work on the moving piston, so energy left as work done, not by cooling.
The heat stored in the gas spread out into a bigger volume, so each part holds less heat.
No energy left the gas; its particles simply moved further apart, so its temperature fell.

questions.stem: An electric kettle heats 250 g of water from 18 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to the water? Ignore energy transferred to the kettle and surroundings.

Water flows through an electric water heater at a steady 0.050 kg s⁻¹. The heater's power is 8.4 kW, and all of it is transferred to the water. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the rise in the water's temperature?
A cylinder contains 0.64 kg of oxygen gas, which consists of O₂ molecules. The molar mass of oxygen atoms is 16 g mol⁻¹, and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many oxygen molecules are in the cylinder?
Damping reduces the amplitude of a mass–spring oscillator from 40 mm to 20 mm. What fraction of the original oscillation energy has been transferred to the surroundings?

options.text: None, because the period has not changed

questions.explanation: E ∝ A². Half the amplitude leaves 1/4 of the energy, so 3/4 has been transferred to the surroundings.

questions.stem: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?

options.text: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.

questions.stem: A sample of ideal gas in a cylinder expands slowly, pushing a piston outward, while its temperature is kept constant. How does the internal energy U_f of the gas at the end of the expansion compare with its internal energy U_i at the start?

options.text: U_f > U_i, since with its atoms further apart the gas stores more potential energy
U_f < U_i, since the gas does work on the piston and loses that much internal energy
They cannot be compared without first knowing how much energy was added to the gas by heating
U_f = U_i, since spacing stores no energy and the atoms' average kinetic energy is unchanged

questions.stem: A 0.300 kg iron block at 80.0 °C is placed in 0.500 kg of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated container, and the block and the water reach a common temperature. The specific heat capacity of iron is 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and the specific heat capacity of water is 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Energy transfer to the container and the surroundings is negligible. What is the common temperature?

A student uses the electrical method to find the specific heat capacity of a brass block. Her value is 10% higher than the data-book value. Which change to her method would most reduce this difference?

options.text: Repeat the experiment three times and calculate a mean value
Use a thermometer with a finer scale, reading to 0.1 °C
Wrap the block in thick insulation and put a lid of insulation on top
Use a lower heater power so the block heats more slowly

questions.explanation: Less energy escapes to the surroundings, so more of VIt raises the block's temperature. The value of c falls towards the true one.

questions.stem: Predict first. Students measure the pressure of three samples of gas, each sealed in a rigid container, at several temperatures between 0 °C and 100 °C. The samples are of different gases and different amounts, and each behaves as an ideal gas. For each sample they plot pressure against temperature in °C and get a straight line. They then extend each best-fit line to zero pressure. What do they find?

options.text: All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, 0 °C.
All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, about −273 °C.
The steepest line reaches zero pressure at the highest temperature.
Each line reaches zero pressure at a temperature set by its kind of gas.
